description:
A passionate team of tech enthusiasts and space explorers building innovative solutions for the future of Mars exploration. We aim to turn Martian data into an interactive survival and navigation guide for future explorers.

Mapping Mars. Preparing Humanity for Beyond Earth.
summary: Marswalk Planner is a Python and Streamlit web app that gives a Mars astronaut one layered map of Jezero Crater for planning a Marswalk (EVA). Users switch between imagery (HiRISE/CTX), elevation (MOLA), thermal (THEMIS) and mineral (CRISM) layers. A slope-hazard overlay is derived from the elevation data. The app plans a slope-aware route to chosen science stops, such as the delta front and carbonate outcrops. It then gives a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict from start time, dust opacity, daylight and suit-time limits
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Marswalk Planner is a web app that helps plan a walk on the Martian surface. It shows one map of Jezero Crater with switchable layers: surface imagery, elevation, temperature and minerals. From the elevation layer it works out how steep the ground is and marks risky slopes, orange above 15° and red above 25°.

The user picks a base and up to three science stops, such as the river delta or a carbonate outcrop. The app finds a walking route that avoids steep ground, and it estimates distance and walking time, since the pace slows on slopes. Two sliders set the start time and the amount of dust in the air. The lighting on the map changes with the time of day. The app then gives a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict, with the reasons written out, based on suit time, daylight, dust and slope.

What are the benefits?

A crew can compare plans quickly. Adding a stop gives more science but costs time and distance, and the app shows that trade immediately. The safety checks happen together on one screen instead of in separate tools.

What impact do we intend?

We want planning a Marswalk to be faster and better informed. We want crews to spend their limited outside hours on the most valuable science without taking avoidable risks. The code is plain Python, so another team could load a different site and reuse it.

What did we use?

  • Language and libraries: Python only, with numpy for the terrain maths, Streamlit and Plotly for the interface and map, and rasterio and GDAL for reading NASA GeoTIFF files.
  • Testing and hosting: pytest for tests, and the app runs locally in a browser.
  • Hardware: an ordinary laptop. No GPU or special equipment is needed.
  • Data: the layers are based on NASA instruments (MOLA, HiRISE and CTX, CRISM, THEMIS, and MEDA/REMS for weather).

Today the app runs on a synthetic terrain that imitates Jezero. We did this on purpose, because real Mars rasters are several gigabytes. A small script crops only the window we need from a real file, and the code reads real GeoTIFFs once they are in the data folder.

How is it creative?

Most Mars viewers show data. This one makes a decision from it. It combines route planning, science targets and a safety verdict in one view, and the map changes with the hour and the dust level.

What did we consider?

  • Crew safety: slope, daylight, suit time and dust storms.
  • Science value: stops are placed where minerals and delta sediments are.
  • Team skills: we chose a Python-only stack that everyone can read.
  • Data size: real files are too large to ship, so we built the crop step.
  • Honesty about limits: the 8-hour suit limit, the slope thresholds and the radiation figure are our own assumptions, not NASA values. The app and slides say so, and they will be replaced with real MEDA, REMS and RAD data.
